This oil deal with Venezuela is absolutely insane.

President Trump just announced that the US has reached a deal to secure "majority control" of over 65 billion barrels of Venezuelan oil reserves.

Furthermore, the US currently has ~46 billion barrels of proven crude oil reserves.

Combined with the 65 billion barrels covered by this agreement, the US would have domestic reserves plus control over ~111 billion barrels of oil.

To put this into perspective, the entire world has roughly 1.57 TRILLION barrels of proven crude oil reserves.

In other words, the US is set to control ~7.1% of all proven oil reserves in the world under this new agreement with Venezuela.

At ~111 billion barrels, the US would be almost exactly in-line with the United Arab Emirates, which has 113 billion barrels of proven crude reserves, and it would exceed Kuwait's 102 billion barrels.

Assuming the agreement is structured as outlined in President Trump’s announcement, the implications for global energy markets will be enormous.

We will publish more in-depth analysis soon.

The US cattle herd fell to 94.2 million head, the lowest in 75 years. Ground beef hit a record $6.69/lb.

Washington is plugging the gap with foreign beef. The White House just added 300,000 tons to the import quota, 4x February's move, and beef imports are up 14% this year.

Imported trimmings buy 90 days. They do not rebuild a herd, which takes years of holding back heifers. A supply shortage keeps beef expensive on the shelf until the cattle come back, and no quota speeds that up.

The revaluation strategy backed by the threat of tariffs has already failed spectacularly. In my view, the decisive reason was that the Trump administration folded first in its trade war with Beijing, with American stores at one point essentially running out of goods.

As a Beijing policy advisor told me a year ago, “We missed the best chance to shift China toward a more consumption-oriented growth model because the US proved too weak (怂).”

Now that China has successfully weathered what was arguably the most aggressive trade war with the US—and its trade surplus continues to surge— I see little reason to believe that tariff threats can force Beijing to rebalance its economy. If anything, the experience may have reinforced the opposite lesson in Beijing: the US lacks the leverage to force China to change its economic model.
